entities.name: Lucius Neratius Priscus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Neratius Priscus, a preeminent Roman senator and jurist, emerged as a pivotal figure in the development of Roman private law during the late 1st and early 2nd centuries CE, a period often regarded as the 'golden age' of classical Roman jurisprudence. As the esteemed head of the Proculeian school, one of the two dominant legal schools in Rome, his interpretations and teachings significantly shaped legal thought. His political career culminated in his service as suffect consul in the nundinium of May–June 97 CE, alongside Marcus Annius Verus, solidifying his status within the Roman elite and granting him legislative influence.

Priscus's primary contribution lay in his profound influence on the evolution of Roman civil law. Although his specific legal writings are not fully extant, his ideas and rulings are extensively cited and discussed by later jurists, particularly by the influential Salvius Julianus, who frequently engaged with Priscus's opinions. Priscus was known for his rigorous adherence to the principles of the Proculeian school, emphasizing a more analytical and systematic approach to legal problems compared to the Sabinian school. His responsa (legal opinions) and institutional commentaries would have guided generations of students and practitioners, contributing to the sophisticated legal framework that characterized the Roman Empire.
